caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 258 of 2001
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam with Shishir Kanti Majumder —For the Appellant. 

M Enayetur Rahim Advocate—For the Respondents.
parties:
Samar Kanti Das Gupta ------ Appellant
vs
Bangladesh Bar Council & another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
20. Ratio stemming from Re Weare, C Sabba Reddi and Rabati Bewa, supra, profess with splendour of wisdom, that in a quasi criminal statutory disciplinary proceedings against an advocate, the phrase "misconduct" may embrace a broader spectrum of actions or omissions—anything that may be treated as "unbecoming of an advocate". It is understandable that acts or omissions occasioned by negligence may, in such proceedings, be encapsulated within the wider definition of the phrase "misconduct", but again, there can be no geminity on the theme that negligence, in the context of such a proceedings, must be reflective of gross or culpable negligence only, the types of negligence, which will permit a person with reasonable perception and prudence, to say that a given advocate was so utterly negligent that it is unsafe and undesirable to allow him to be entrusted with other people's affairs. Simple or inculpable negligence can certainly not lead to such a conclusion and hence such negligence cannot warrant infliction of punishment of a dimension that may drag the accused to far reaching consequences not only in respect to his reputation but also on his very livelihood. The question as to what sort of negligence should be treated as "gross" in order to ignite the apparatus of criminal law, was succinctly yet, lucidly, replied to by Hewart CJ in R vs Batemam (1925 94 LJKB) who sermoned that negligence to be the basis in a criminal charge, must be a gross one in the sense that it went beyond mere matter of compensation between subjects. The House of Lords in the modern and sensational case of R vs Adomako (1994 1 WLR 15), described with precision the required degree of culpable negligence by observing, that the question to be asked is whether, having regard to the risk involved, the conduct of the accused was so bad in all the circumstances as to amount to a criminal act or omission. Nobody can sensibly argue that the principles pertaining to mens rea which were considered in full-fledged criminal cases, should be followed squarely with the same degree of obstinacy and rigidity in a proceeding of quasi criminal nature of the Bar Council. But it would be outrageous to say that an advocate should be deprived of his bread and butter for a conduct which is not a foetus either of his diabolic state of mind or that of his reprehensible negligence. Thus, even when it is proved that an advocate furnished inaccurate opinion, without proof of guilty mind, recklessness or gross negligence, the gap between the cup and the lips must still remain wide enough to thwart any attempt to pour the unpalatable substance of retribution. 

 24. Mr Rahim, in his best of endeavours to sway us, said that it is often impossible to procure witness to depose on what went on in the discreet area of an advocate's chamber. Is it really so? Usually a client visits his advocate's chamber with some companions. His co-travellers can, in most cases, be formidable witnesses. The clients should also, for their best interest, insist upon written opinion and advice because, irrespective of the nature and the forum of the proceedings, he has to prove his allegation by credible evidence. Be that as it may, the accuser's inability to procure evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, cannot justify dispensation with the rule "Probandi necessitas," the requirement of adducing of evidence to prove a charge the accuser laid. Such a leverage will create a havoc on the entire populace, leading to judicial nightmare. True it is, that we ought not to remain blind-folded in the wake of frightful escalation in the instances of misconduct. It is equally true—and to that extent we are in wholesome consensus with Mr Rahim—that firm, resolute and, if necessary, merciless approach should be adopted to contain spiral hike of such loathsome incidents. Such objectives can be achieved by allowing flexibility in the standard of proof, definitely not by jettisoning the safety valve that shields innocent victims against vexatious accusation. It has to be clutched in mind that finding of guilt on mere speculation, howsoever strong the speculative perception may be, is not only alien to our jurisprudence, but is also repugnant to civilised norm. 

 25. Generally a charge of criminal or quasi criminal nature is to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, but as Denning, J (as he then was) in Miller vs Minister of Pension (1947 2 All ER 372), emphasised, "beyond reasonable doubt" does not mean "beyond shadow of doubt," and as he (by then a Lord Justice) pronounced in Bater vs Bater, (1950 2 All ER 458) that standard of proof may fluctuate depending on what is at stake. Hence, in the prevalence of dreadful soaring in the occurrences of professional misconduct, the weight of proof in disciplinary proceedings against advocates and, of course, members of similar professional bodies, may desirably be relaxed to an acceptable proportion. But proving an allegation with a lighter burden of proof is one thing, and adducing no evidence at all, is quite another. In the instant case, there was simply no evidence to substantiate the charges recorded in the indictment. It is to be added that an advocate instructed to simply draft a bainanama undertakes no suo motu obligation to conduct search on the title to the property, and nothing in the Bar Council rules proscribes drafting of bainanama.
